title: Asset Allocation
blurb: How a client's money is split between equity, debt, gold and cash: setting the mix, explaining it and keeping it on target.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays) and investors as awareness material
One 60–75 minute session, plus 20 minutes of role-play and the quiz
Module 6 (bonds and debt), Module 9 (goal-based investing), Module 11 (the wrong time to invest) and Module 12 (SIP – What Next?)
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway
outcomes: Explain asset allocation in one sentence, and why it matters more than fund selection.
Describe how equity, debt, gold and cash behave, and why mixing them helps.
Assess risk capacity, risk tolerance and time horizon before suggesting a mix.
Build an illustrative mix for a goal and choose suitable products for each part.
Rebalance when the mix drifts, and adjust it as life changes.
Handle the behaviour that breaks allocations, and stay within compliance.

sources: Angel One: Nifty 50 versus gold, including 2008 (Nifty about −52%, gold in rupees about +27%)
SEBI circular on categorisation of multi-asset allocation funds (at least 10% in each of at least three asset classes)
SEBI riskometer and Potential Risk Class circulars; AMFI best-practices on risk profiling
Income-tax Act and Finance Act provisions on capital gains and debt-fund taxation (verify current rates each year)

lessons.title: The four asset classes and their jobs
Two ways to hold a mix
Capacity vs tolerance: build for the lower
Step 1: the horizon sets the equity range
Step 2: the risk profile picks a point
What the mix means in rupees
Drift and the rules of rebalancing
When to change the target mix

a: The best mix is the one the client can stick with through a bad year.
Deciding what share of money goes into each asset class, based on goals, horizon and ability to handle losses.
The mix explains most of how much a portfolio swings over time; it is the first decision, before choosing funds.
Equity (growth), debt (stability and income), gold (diversifier), cash (liquidity).
Nifty 50 fell about 52%; gold in rupees rose about 27%. Assets don't move together.
Time horizon, risk capacity, risk tolerance, goal type. The market view is not an input.
Capacity = financial ability to bear losses; tolerance = emotional willingness. Build for the lower one.
Emergency fund, near goals and long goals each get their own mix.
EPF, PPF, FDs, gold, property belong in the total picture; EPF and PPF are debt.
Conservative 30/60/10; moderate 50/40/10; aggressive 70/20/10 (equity/debt/gold).
₹10 L for 15 years: FD ≈ ₹25.7 L; conservative ≈ ₹34.5 L; moderate ≈ ₹39.6 L; aggressive ≈ ₹45.3 L.
SEBI requires at least 10% in each of at least three asset classes.
Check yearly; act if drift exceeds about 5 points; use new money first; check exit loads and tax.
A goal within 3–5 years, a life event, or a new risk profile; never a market view.
Ownership in companies; the growth engine.
Example: flexi-cap, index, mid-cap funds.
Remember: highest long-run growth, sharp falls.
Lending for interest; the stabiliser.
Example: short-duration, gilt, corporate bond funds; PPF, EPF.
Remember: has rate and credit risk; not risk-free.
A diversifier that often holds up in crises.
Example: gold ETFs, gold funds.
Remember: 5–15% is usually enough.
Money for liquidity and emergencies.
Example: savings account, liquid funds.
Remember: often below inflation after tax.
The long-term target mix.
Example: 60/30/10 for a 10-year goal.
Remember: set from goals and risk profile.
The mix moving away from target as markets move.
Example: 60/40 becomes 65/35 after a strong year.
Remember: normal; fix it with rules.
Bringing the mix back to target.
Example: move 5 points from equity to debt.
Remember: sells high, buys low, automatically.
Rebalance when drift passes a set limit.
Example: act at 5 points away from target.
Remember: removes emotion from timing.
Financial ability to bear losses.
Example: stable income, no loans, big buffer.
Remember: can be high while tolerance is low.
Emotional willingness to bear losses.
Example: sold everything in the 2020 fall.
Remember: ask in rupees, not percentages.
Broad core funds plus small higher-risk holdings.
Example: 80% flexi/index, 20% mid/small/thematic.
Remember: keep satellites small.
One fund holding three or more asset classes.
Example: equity, debt and gold in one scheme.
Remember: at least 10% in each (SEBI).
A hybrid fund that changes its equity-debt mix dynamically.
Example: equity share moves with valuations.
Remember: check the actual mix in the factsheet.
Moving money into last year's best asset.
Example: "Gold did 20%, move it all."
Remember: each asset has its year.
Treating some money as separate from the rest.
Example: "EPF doesn't count."
Remember: count all assets in the mix.
Too much in one stock, sector or property.
Example: most wealth in employer shares.
Remember: diversify new money around it.

questions.q: What is asset allocation?
o: Deciding what share of money goes into each asset class
questions.why: It is the split across asset classes, decided before choosing any fund.

questions.q: Which asset class is mainly for long-term growth?
questions.why: Equity has the highest long-run growth, with sharp falls along the way.

questions.q: In 2008, roughly how did the Nifty 50 and gold in rupees move?
questions.why: They moved in opposite directions, which is why mixing helps.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four inputs that set the mix?
questions.why: The mix comes from the client, not from a market view.

questions.q: A client has high risk capacity but low risk tolerance. What do you build for?
questions.why: Always build for the lower of the two.

questions.q: Money needed within a year should be in…
questions.why: Under a year means no equity: liquid, overnight or money-market funds.

questions.q: For a 7+ year goal, an illustrative moderate mix is…
questions.why: Moderate is 50% equity, 40% debt, 10% gold, as a teaching example.

questions.q: SEBI requires a multi-asset allocation fund to hold…
o: At least 10% in each of at least three asset classes
questions.why: That is the multi-asset mandate.

questions.q: A 60/40 portfolio becomes 65/35 after a strong equity year. What does rebalancing involve?
o: Moving about 5 points from equity to debt
questions.why: Return to target by booking some equity gains.

questions.q: What is usually the cheapest way to rebalance?
o: Directing new money to the underweight asset
questions.why: New money avoids exit loads and tax on a sale.

questions.q: A client has ₹25 lakh in EPF and calls himself "100% equity". What should you do?
o: Count EPF as debt in his total mix
Ask him to close the EPF
questions.why: EPF is debt. Counting everything may mean the funds can hold more equity than the standalone view suggested.

questions.q: Which is a good reason to change the target mix?
o: A goal is now within 3 years
questions.why: Goals, life events and a changed risk profile justify a new target.

questions.q: Gold's main role in a portfolio is…
o: A diversifier that often holds up when equity falls
questions.why: Gold is a diversifier; usually 5–15% is enough.

questions.q: In the ₹10 L, 15-year illustration, the moderate mix reached about…
questions.why: About ₹39.6 L at the assumed returns; not a forecast.

questions.q: Which statement is compliant?
o: "Illustratively, at assumed returns, this mix could reach about ₹40 L; not guaranteed."
questions.why: Label the projection illustrative, state the assumption, promise nothing.

questions.q: True or false: the right mix can be decided from the market outlook alone.
questions.why: It comes from horizon, capacity, tolerance and goal type — never from a market view.

questions.q: True or false: one client can need different mixes for different goals.
questions.why: Separate pots, separate mixes: emergency fund, near goals and long goals each get their own.

questions.q: True or false: debt funds carry no risk at all.
o: Only if held for three years
questions.why: Debt funds carry interest-rate and credit risk. They are not risk-free.

questions.q: True or false: rebalancing after a fall can mean buying equity at lower prices.
questions.why: Restoring the target moves money from debt to equity after a fall.

questions.q: True or false: a mixed portfolio cannot fall in value.
questions.why: It usually falls less than pure equity, but it can fall.

questions.q: Mrs. Kulkarni, 52, keeps ₹30 lakh in FDs for retirement at 60 and wants no risk. What is the right approach?
o: Explain inflation risk with illustrative numbers, profile her, suggest a conservative mix
Put it all in equity to catch up
questions.why: Inflation risk, a proper risk profile, a conservative mix, and no promises.

questions.q: Vikram wants to move his whole portfolio into gold after a strong year. What do you do?
o: Explain that each asset has its year and keep gold to the agreed share
questions.why: Gold is a diversifier: keep it to the agreed share, often 5–15%.

questions.q: Neha, 29, has her wedding fund (needed in 18 months) in a small-cap fund. What is the plan?
o: Leave it; small caps do well over time
Separate pot: move to short-duration debt on a plan, check the exit load
Move it to another small-cap fund
questions.why: Money needed in 18 months belongs in debt or liquid funds, whatever its long-term potential.

questions.q: A 60/40 client is at 66/34 after a strong year and refuses to sell equity. Best next step?
o: Explain the band rule, use new money for debt first, and record the decision
questions.why: Use the agreed rules: new money first, partial rebalance if needed, documented.

questions.q: A moderate client wants 100% debt after equity fell 20%. Best response?
o: Move everything to debt as asked
Show how the mix cushioned the fall and rebalance per the agreed rules
Promise equity will recover next year
questions.why: Show the mix working, review goal and profile, follow the rules, make no predictions.

questions.q: What is the one line to remember from this module?
o: The best mix is the one the client can stick with through a bad year
questions.why: A mix the client abandons in a fall does worse than a modest mix they hold.

questions.q: What is cash's job in the mix?
questions.why: Cash is for liquidity, so nothing long-term has to be sold at the wrong moment.

questions.q: What is the band rule?
o: Rebalance when drift passes a set limit, such as 5 points
Buy only within a price band
questions.why: A pre-agreed drift limit that triggers rebalancing without emotion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason to change the target mix?
o: A new loan or a child's birth
questions.why: Market performance alone never changes the target.

questions.q: What does rebalancing quietly do?
questions.why: Returning to the target trims what has run up and tops up what has fallen.
